analysis.one_liner: Conditions federal financing for manufactured home parks on tenant protections, including rent-increase notice.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Banking Committee — it got no hearing, no markup, and no vote, and expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Millions of Americans own their manufactured home but rent the land under it, and can face large lot-rent increases or sudden closure. This bill would make community owners promise baseline tenant protections — one-year renewable leases, 60-day advance written notice of rent increases with a written justification, a grace period and cure period before eviction for late rent, the right to sell the home in place, 60-day notice before a community is sold or closed, and penalties for violations — as a condition of getting federally insured or Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac-financed loans to build, rehabilitate, or buy manufactured home communities. It would apply those protections across every community an owner holds, not just the financed one, and create a commission to propose stronger standards.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of manufactured home communities — people who usually own their home but rent the pad it sits on. They would get advance notice and written justification before rent or new charges are added, more time to cure late rent, the right to sell their home in place rather than pay to move it, notice and a 60-day window to negotiate before a community is sold or shut down, and financial penalties paid to them when owners violate the rules [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Manufactured home residents who rent their lots

how_it_helps.text: A borrower cannot get HUD-insured or Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac-financed financing for building, substantially rehabilitating, or purchasing a manufactured home community unless the owner commits to minimum protections in leases, including one-year renewable leases and 60-day written notice of rent increases or new charges, with written justification of the increase [S2] [S3].

The protections apply to leases across every manufactured home community the borrower or an affiliate owns, not only the property being financed, so the owner cannot comply at one park while raising rents elsewhere [S3].
Rent increases above 5 percent trigger extra advance notice — an additional 30 days for each additional 2.5 percent increase — giving residents more warning as hikes get larger [S3].

Residents gain a 5-day rent grace period, a right to cure default within 15 days, the right to sell their home in place even after eviction, the right to post For Sale signs, and 60-day advance notice of a sale or closure, during which the owner must negotiate in good faith if tenants want to buy the community [S2] [S3].
Violations carry penalties paid to the injured tenant — for example, repayment of an improper rent increase with interest plus 25 percent, or six months of rent for wrongful termination [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Manufactured home community owners and investors — including large institutional buyers — bear the cost: they must embed the protections in leases, document compliance, justify rent increases in writing, and pay statutory penalties to tenants when they violate the rules. Some owners could face slower or smaller rent increases, and lenders and Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac would take on enforcement duties, which could make some community financing harder or costlier to obtain [S2] [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Community owners, investors, and their lenders

drawbacks.text: The protections attach only to federally backed financing, so communities owned without HUD insurance or Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac loans are untouched, leaving many residents without the new rights [S2] [S3].

Making financing conditional could make it harder or more expensive for some community owners — including small operators or tenant groups trying to buy their parks — to get loans for purchases and improvements, since lenders and the housing enterprises would have to verify lease compliance before buying loans [S3].

The bill directs no new funding and relies on HUD and the Federal Housing Finance Agency to absorb oversight and enforcement costs from existing budgets, raising questions about how thoroughly compliance would actually be checked [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The tenant protections are modest, well-targeted, and modeled on standards Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac already require for the specific properties they finance — this bill would extend similar terms to every community an owner holds and add real penalties. The main cost falls on owners' flexibility to raise lot rents without justification, which is exactly the practice the bill aims to curb. The honest caveat is coverage: because the bill works only through federal loan programs, it protects residents of financed communities, not all of them, and conditioning financing could add friction to some community sales and purchases.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Jeanne Shaheen introduced the Manufactured Housing Tenant's Bill of Rights Act of 2023 on June 22, 2023, joined by Senators Blumenthal and Fetterman; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs [S1] [S5].
The action history shows no further activity after the referral — no hearing, no committee report, no floor vote [S5].
Only three senators sponsored or cosponsored the bill, all Democrats, and no companion action is recorded in the House [S4] [S5].
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and bills not passed by both chambers expire at the end of a Congress, so the bill died in committee without ever coming to a vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners and investors of manufactured home communities, especially large institutional buyers, are better off because the bill died: they face no federal baseline of lease protections, no written justification requirement for rent increases, and no tenant penalties. Lenders and the housing enterprises are also spared new enforcement duties. Residents of manufactured home communities, who often have little bargaining power once a large owner buys their park, got nothing.

industries.industry: Manufactured home community owners and investors (including institutional and private-equity buyers)
industries.note: The bill conditions access to federal financing on lease protections, written justification for rent increases, and tenant penalties — directly limiting the flexibility that lets owners raise lot rents on residents who own their homes but not the land. Large investors who have consolidated parks and raised lot rents would bear most of the constraint.

industries.industry: Mortgage lenders and housing finance enterprises (Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac, HUD-insured lending)
industries.note: Lenders lose some loan volume and gain compliance work, since loans are eligible only if the borrower certifies tenant protections and documents compliance. They also gain a standardized site lease designed to keep manufactured homes eligible for the enterprises' single-family mortgage programs.

industries.industry: Manufactured home buyers and sellers (residents who own their homes)
industries.note: Residents gain the right to sell their home in place without relocating it, to post For Sale signs, and to assign the pad lease to a buyer, which protects the resale value of what is often a family's largest asset.
